newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew change crashed computer part, do tests.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew change crashed computer part, do tests.

text.p: The crew of Russia's Mir space station, drifting in orbit after their computer broke down, successfully replaced a faulty part of the system and plan to reboot the computer on Wednesday, a Mission Control official said on Tuesday.

"They have changed the system block that malfunctioned and are about to start testing the system," Viktor Blagov, deputy flight head, told Reuters from the Mission Control at the town of Korolyov outside Moscow.
He said the test results would be available in the evening.

"We may find out that more computer sections need to be replaced," Blagov said. "Otherwise, the cosmonauts will try to switch on the computer system on Wednesday and restore Mir's stable alignment to the sun."
Mir has to be constantly aligned to the sun for its solar panels to produce energy.
Blagov said the cosmonauts, two Russians and an American, would have to realign the station as quickly as possible to avoid running down the batteries, which are needed to run the computer system.
"Orientation should be recovered as soon as the computer system starts working. But they have to do it quickly."

The station has been spinning in orbit since Monday evening, when the computer failure during a docking procedure between Mir and a cargo ship prompted the station automatically to switch off all but vital life support systems.
Blagov said the cosmonauts might take a spacewalk to Mir's damaged airless Spektr module on Thursday, one day later than the sortie had been initiallly scheduled.

"Once they have the computer running and solar panels oriented to the sun, they can go to Spektr," Blagov said, adding that the sortie could be postponed until Friday or later if the first attempt to reboot the system is not successful.
"So we are prepared to abort the attempt (to reboot the computer) and switch off the system again if we see that they are running low on batteries," Blagov said.

Mir has run on partial power since Spektr was holed in a collision with a cargo ship on June 25 in the worst accident in its 11-year history. The cosmonauts have to enter the module to reconnect electric cables leading from Spektr's solar panels to the main ship.
Blagov also complained that a lack of cash was behind Monday's computer crash as Russians had to use Mir equipment until it virtually falls apart.

"We are saving a lot of money on this scheme, but we really have to decide soon whether we need safety or money-saving," he said. The broken computer unit, which exchanges data between all peripheral system parts and the computer centre, had not been changed for almost 11 years, Blagov added.
"This interface malfunctioned. Unfortunately it happened during a docking procedure. During a routine flight there would be no consequences, but now we have problems," Blagov said.
Despite difficult conditions, Mir's commander Anatoly Solovyov managed to complete the docking of a supply ship manually without incident.

It was the third time the station had spun out of control in less than two months and came as a blow to the new Russian crew, which had enjoyed a relatively trouble-free start to their mission after their predecessors suffered a string of disasters.
Blagov said the cosmonauts had to fire engines of their Soyuz spaceship to turn the station a bit every time it was reaching a position when solar panels could not catch sunlight.

"We see from the earth when power supply is low and we tell them to go to their spaceship and fire the engines for 10 seconds," Blagov said, adding that now the spinning station was getting enough solar rays to keep life support systems working.
